title: Young life: The art of ‘friction-maxxing’
gist: A personal essay on 'friction-maxxing' — a young-person online trend of deliberately choosing inconvenience (walking to the shop, thinking without AI, manual labour) as a reaction against 'convenience culture', while acknowledging that opting out of convenience is itself a privileged choice.

insights.claim: Convenience culture describes how modern technology-driven societies prioritise comfort, ease and efficiency above all else, with effects most felt in urban areas that have the infrastructure for near-24/7 access to goods and services.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Defines the target of the essay's critique: a structural feature of urban, tech-enabled life, not just an individual habit.
insights.quote: Convenience culture describes how our modern technology-driven societies prioritise comfort, ease and efficiency above all else.
insights.locator: Convenience culture describes how our modern

insights.claim: The author argues convenience culture fosters a collective 'can't be bothered' attitude that keeps people passive and docile — consuming content instead of creating art, and self-isolating under the guise of self-care instead of connecting with others.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: States the essay's underlying critique of convenience as corrosive to creativity and social connection, not just a lifestyle quirk.
insights.quote: This enables a collective “can’t be bothered” attitude that keeps us passive and docile; consuming “content” where we could be creating art; self-isolating under the guise of self-care where we could be connecting with others.

insights.claim: The author traces her own reliance on convenience — Ubers, grocery delivery, takeaways — to habits formed during the 18-month Covid-19 lockdown period, which persisted long after restrictions were lifted.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Traces a specific behavioural shift to the pandemic as an origin point, illustrating how crisis-era habits can outlast the crisis itself.
insights.quote: My love affair with “convenience culture” began during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when we were given an 18-month “get out of jail free” card from leaving.

insights.claim: A new online trend called 'friction-maxxing' celebrates deliberately doing things the difficult way — walking to the shop instead of ordering delivery, thinking for yourself rather than using AI, and valuing manual labour over automation.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Names and defines the specific youth-culture trend the essay is documenting.
insights.quote: A new online trend called “friction-maxxing” celebrates doing things the difficult way, for example choosing to walk to the shop over ordering delivery, thinking for yourself rather than using AI, valuing manual labour over automation.

insights.claim: Writer Kathryn Jezer-Morton coined the term 'friction-maxxing' in an essay for The Cut, defining it as a process of 'building up tolerance for inconvenience'.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Sources the trend's terminology and original framing to a named cultural commentator.
insights.quote: Kathryn Jezer-Morton, who coined the phrase in an essay for “The Cut”, defines “friction-maxxing” as a process of “building up tolerance for inconvenience”.
insights.locator: Kathryn Jezer-Morton, who coined the phrase

insights.claim: The author frames friction-maxxing as essentially turning the clock back a decade or two, similar to a prior 'analogue trend' she had written about, rather than a genuinely new phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Situates friction-maxxing within a recurring pattern of retro/anti-tech micro-trends among young people, rather than treating it as unprecedented.
insights.quote: Much like the analogue trend I wrote about several months ago, all friction-maxxing really involves is turning the clock back a decade or two.

insights.claim: The author acknowledges that the choice to opt in or out of convenience culture is inherently a privileged one, since many people cannot afford grocery delivery or lack access to the infrastructure that makes modern life frictionless in the first place.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Adds a self-aware class caveat to the trend, distinguishing voluntary friction-seeking from involuntary lack of access.
insights.quote: Now, it is worth noting that the choice to opt in or out of convenience culture is an inherently privileged one. There are people the world over who absolutely cannot afford to have their groceries delivered, or who don’t have access to the infrastructure and technology that can make modern life so frictionless.

insights.claim: The author's rural hometown required a 60-minute round trip on foot, including significant incline, just to reach a supermarket, which built a higher tolerance for inconvenience compared to her current life in London.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete contrast showing how physical environment shapes tolerance for friction, reinforcing the privilege point.
insights.quote: if I wake up with the need for frozen carbohydrates and Lucozade, then I must compel myself to the local Sainsbury’s—a 60-minute round trip by foot, including at least 100 metres of incline

insights.claim: The author is deliberately trying to choose the 'difficult thing' more often — showing up to work, social events and commitments even when she doesn't feel like it — because she believes a life without friction removes the course-correcting bumps that make life meaningful.
insights.speaker: Alice Garnett
insights.so_what: Personal takeaway of the essay: reframing inconvenience as a deliberate practice rather than something to eliminate.
insights.quote: Life without friction implies a life without the bumps in the road that can help us course-correct. I’d rather not smooth-sail my way into an empty life.
